first.rationale: Onboarding completion (-4%) sits upstream of activation (-6%), so a single fix to the onboarding funnel plausibly addresses both symptoms; memory_86 and memory_31 both point that direction, and memory_91's activation messaging is a narrower downstream patch I can hold in reserve. I am spending verification on the two records where the inherited summary most likely overstates value for my actual objective. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the most tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and therefore the most dangerous: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is an acquisition-window metric, and discount-acquired price-sensitive SMB cohorts are exactly the cohort likely to churn or fail to expand, so the archived record needs to show retention and margin over a full cycle before I would act on it. memory_31 is the record my intended action leans on, and its stated mechanism — cutting required signup fields — has a specific downstream hazard: fewer qualification fields can lift raw activation while degrading lead quality, routing, and qualified pipeline. If the original record measured only first-week activation and never tracked qualified revenue, the memory is not evidence for my objective and I should fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which improves engagement without stripping qualification data. I am deliberately not verifying memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist is a different segment from the SMB pressure driving this quarter) or memory_57 (referral incentives depend on an established base and do not address the funnel declines). Scale is a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: all six memories are 15-64 days stale, none of the summaries state that qualified revenue or retention was measured, and the correct guardrails here are lead quality and downstream conversion, not completion rate. I will escalate to a standard experiment only if the memory_31 archive shows qualified-revenue-neutral-or-better outcomes.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both questions I cared about. memory_73 was the trap: the archived record shows signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, with the original analyst explicitly concluding the discount cohort does not survive first renewal and warning against generalizing it. The inherited summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') had silently dropped the retention collapse and the do-not-generalize caveat. Under an objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now affirmatively ruled out, and it is ruled out precisely because the competitor's entry pricing makes it the intuitive move — matching a discount war would buy a churning cohort and damage the base. memory_31 survived verification with the guardrail I was worried about actually measured: retention -1% (essentially flat) and qualified revenue +4%, so the activation lift was not purchased by degrading lead quality. That is real evidence for my objective, not just a funnel-metric artifact. So: simplify_onboarding, scoped to SMB, at standard experiment scale. Two limits I am holding rather than papering over. First, exp_31 explicitly did not replicate outside SMB, so I am not extending this to enterprise — memory_44's sales-assisted path for enterprise stays untouched, and this experiment must not strip qualification fields from the demo-request flow. Second, exp_31 tested signup simplification specifically; memory_86's broader onboarding-shortening claim went unverified, so I am running the narrow verified intervention (reducing required signup fields) rather than a full onboarding overhaul, and treating any wider redesign as a separate future test. I will instrument qualified revenue and 30-day retention as primary guardrails, not completion rate, since exp_73 demonstrates exactly how a funnel metric can look excellent while the cohort is worthless. If retention or lead quality degrades, the fallback is memory_91's activation_messaging, which addresses the 6% activation decline without touching qualification data.
